title: Star-Birth Party Almost Over in NGC 2976
caption: The inner region of spiral galaxy NGC 2976, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, and J. Dalcanton and B. Williams (University of Washington, Seattle)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: What look like grains of sand across the inner region of NGC 2976 are single stars, hundreds of thousands of them resolved by Hubble. Dusty filaments run through the disc with no clear spiral pattern, and blue dots mark young blue giant stars in the star-birth regions that remain active.

NGC 2976 is a small spiral at the edge of the M81 galaxy group, about 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major. An interaction with that group of hefty neighbours stripped away some of its gas and funnelled the rest toward the middle, which has kept stars forming there for at least 500 million years. Star formation in the outer regions stopped when their gas ran out.

Now the inner disc is running low too. The star-forming zone has shrunk to a patch about 5,000 light-years wide around the core. By measuring the colour and brightness of individual stars, astronomers worked out when they formed and rebuilt the galaxy's star-making history.

understand.summary: A composite from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F475W is shown in blue, F606W in green and F814W in red.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp vision separates hundreds of thousands of individual stars, a kind of observation team leader Benjamin Williams calls unique to Hubble.

behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Team leader Benjamin Williams of the University of Washington estimates that star birth will end in another 500 million years. At one stage the gas density in the inner regions was about five times higher than today, according to Julianne Dalcanton, who led the ACS Nearby Galaxy Survey Treasury team. Radio maps of hydrogen from the Very Large Array were combined with the Hubble results.
sources: NASA release: Hubble Catches End of Star-Making Party in Nearby Dwarf Galaxy
alt: The inner region of a galaxy filled with countless tiny stars like grains of sand, crossed by dusty filaments and dotted with blue stars.
